L26@P1: Abstract—Smart Contracts (SC for short) are gaining momentum as a suitable technology for ensuring trusted execution
L27@P1: of Business Processes (BP for short) in open environment.
L28@P1: Nevertheless, the transactional semantics of SC which follow
L29@P1: ACID transactions are not appropriate for BP characteristics.
L30@P1: Indeed, it is admitted that ACID transactions are limited
L31@P1: to cope with complex control structure and long running
L32@P1: execution of BP. Transactional Business Processes (TBP for
L33@P1: short) have emerged as an extension to ACID models to
L34@P1: overcome these limits. A TBP ensures transactional reliability
L35@P1: of advanced transactions having a control structure as complex
L36@P1: as for BP. In this paper, we propose an approach that builds on
L37@P1: SC and extends them to implement TBP. We extend Caterpillar,
L38@P1: an existing BP execution engine developed on top of Ethereum,
L39@P1: to implement our approach and support the execution of TBP.

L42@P1: I. INTRODUCTION
L43@P1: The advent of the Blockchain technology with its two
L44@P1: generations created in last years a huge amount of interest
L45@P1: across various industries and academic communities due
L46@P1: to its mechanisms to ensure trust in open and distributed
L47@P1: execution environments . The first generation of blockchain
L48@P1: allows only sending and receiving monetary values of
L49@P1: cryptocurrencies such as the Bitcoin. While the second
L50@P1: generation, also called the Smart Contracts (SC) blockchain,
L51@P1: enables more complex applications like a valid car sale,
L52@P1: a loan assessment, voting or health care tracking. A SC

L33: ## Preamble
L34: The digital age promised permanence and delivered ephemerality. Humans accumulated identity credentials across hundreds of accounts, memories across dozens of platforms, authorizations in opaque permission dialogs, relationships in proprietary graphs, assets in institutional silos, health records in incompatible portals, family archives in rented cloud buckets, and legacy intentions in scattered documents no executor can locate. Each system claims to store something for the human.
L35: None stores everything under human authority. None persists across vendor failure. None inherits without institutional gatekeeping. None answers a single question with integrity: Who owns this life, and who controls access to it?
L36: Ownership without secure repository is theoretical. Sovereignty without encrypted persistence is rhetorical. Memory without governed retention is liability. Inheritance without vault architecture is chaos. The Human Sovereignty Charter establishes rights — ownership, control, portability, inspectability, deletion, revocation, inheritance. Rights require architecture that implements them when platforms dissolve, devices fail, humans die, and agents multiply.
L37: This document defines the Trust Vault — the foundational secure repository architecture through which Keyra Companions, Human Digital Twins, Life Graphs, Family Trust Networks, Organization Graphs, KAAI-authorized agents, and future digital economies access, protect, and transmit human digital life under explicit constitutional governance.
